item.content:encoded:
I deliberately set out to draw parallels with Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs. I had just finished the game feeling the atmosphere was amazing but the gameplay was pretty boring and the ending kind of uninspired. We KNOW what's coming long before it does.

My own inspiration was exploring the earlier levels. Everything is ominously quiet and empty, and the windows were opaqued by gray fog. I imagined Oswald having teleported his home to some kind of limbo to protect his children after his wife died. My own narrator is that kind of character.

I also wanted to tie different canons together in subtle ways. In my own canon, the Worm is both the Factory and the Broken God, a being that is straining to be "born" or built by human hands so it can exist in this reality. But what isn't clear is whether the Worm is a separate entity or something born in our collective consciousness and pieced together by divided minds unsure of what one another is doing, but all unknowingly working towards the same goal.

item.content:encoded:
Staff, I'll collapse this in a minute when I find the coding and don't screw it up.

+ literary rant
- precious eagle cactus fruit help us

I sure did like it! I actually love it - I've been thinking about it all day, which is always a sign that a work of fiction is powerful enough to stick with me.

I did have another thought about A Machine for Pigs' relation to it, though. It's not a negative thing, per se - just a connection I made.

I think that when you wrote this after playing Amnesia, what stuck in your mind consciously was the environment (a machine, a lantern, monsters), but something deeper stuck subconsciously. (Warning: incoming literary rant.)

*steps onto game psychology podium*

Well, how do I start… put it this way: A Machine for Pigs is a very powerful narrative1 in terms of symbolism and I guess allegory too on a wide scale, though that may sound obvious/redundant.

I saw some similarities in terms of said symbolism between The Worm and A Machine for Pigs that went, I think, way beyond the environment and setting as previously mentioned.

  • Both have to do with a mortal man (the protagonist) allegorically discovering the darker side of both himself and humankind through uncanny or supernatural means.
  • Though your story is set a tad bit past the industrial revolution while A Machine for Pigs is set in the heart of it, both narratives have to do with machinery and industry representing the discovery of said darker side of man. As the industrial revolution was a time period that caused panic and concern regarding the fast development of industry, it is a fitting setting for said existential conflict in the main characters.
  • Both stories revolve around said mortal man/main character sacrificing his humanity and compassion (represented in both narratives by his child(ren)) for personal exploration or self-actualization (Oswald's knowledge of his own past and the machine, your protagonist's realization and acceptance of the fact that he is symbolically the worm).
  • And finally, both stories have 'enemies', if you'll pardon my video game word, that are representative of mindless following of a corrupt cause by creatures/humans that were only brought to their current standing by some action of the protagonist that went horribly wrong. Wretches2 are massively screwed-up versions of slaughterhouse pigs (the failure of Oswald's processing plant due to his amnesia) while the creatures in The Worm are massively screwed-up versions of the protagonist's original followers (the failure of his worm-containment machine due to his general state of madness and disillusionment).

Soooo…. yeah. I think the folks at Frictional would laugh at that, as they were probably just trying to make a gory horror game. Oh well, I did it all anyway.

TL;DR: The general overview is that your Amnesia-inspired work was Amnesia-inspired because of the setting, but I would argue that the setting was simply a cloak for the shared philosophical aspects of the game and the story.

Footnotes
1. The Dark Descent is a better game, I'd venture to say (I mean, not running out of oil in A Machine for Pigs kind of ruined some of the stress) but the entire story is that Daniel is a torturer who screwed up his life and now he's gonna go kill a guy. There's no depth there.
2. E: it has come to my attention that the enemies in AMFP are commonly known as 'Manpigs.' No. Wretches4life, Wretches4ever, Wretches were first.

I go to throw the switch of my great machine, and free ourselves from the madness of the grave.

Okay, I legitimately thought that The Chinese Room and Frictional had borrowed from this, not the other way around. I also didn't expect the first comment to be what I was thinking, as I figured this tale was older than A Machine for Pigs.

You know, even though I feel that this might borrow a little too heavily from that, it's still a brilliant story with brilliant diction and tone.

Also,

Hastily I scribbled down designs that had been burned into my mind, strange and alien architectures I did not recognize or understand.

Something like that reportedly happened to Nikola Tesla, who was, by the way, a badass.

Yeah. Between the Amnesia-ish stuff, the relation to Tesla, and the edgy-and-dark steampunk world I envisioned, this earns all my cool points. Upvote times five.

item.content:encoded:
I like that, 1678 certainly matches the tone and atmosphere very well. Hmmm…let's see…
Might be that some of the cultists managed to survive and learn to avoid the worm-maddened mechanical monstrosities. With time, they even managed to tame a portion of the prison-device into a rough reflection of their nearly-forgotten home. For a while, they thrived in the security of their constructed pseudo-London, trusting in the wind-up "bobbies" to keep them safe.

But the corruption of the Worm is insidious and implacable. The beginning of the end was a single small "bird", a sparrow with wings of rusted iron. In contrast to the silently vigilant camera-pigeons the sparrow's gears clashed and ground against each other. Its song was the scream of tortured metal. One bird was soon two, then a flock, until the streetlights were hidden behind the blur of their flitting casings and the pattern of their screams drilled away at even the stoutest sanity.

The city council only realized the true depth of the threat when it was too late. As psychosis spread like gangrene, they activated The Project. The Project was the center of all unLondon science and industry, an attempt to invert the device that brought the First Fathers to limbo. It was far from ready. But the council, feeling the beginnings of the Pattern Screamer madness themselves, flipped the switch anyway. And it worked! …after a fashion. The Project brought unLondon out of Limbo and safely back into the real world; it just didn't bring the residents along. Back in Limbo, the suddenly refuge-less citizens of unLondon are now nothing but grisly lubricant in the gears of the Worm's abandoned minions.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I think I'm going to go with an all-of-the-above head canon on this one.

By sheer chance some of the workers were not there when the machine was turned on. The "miraculous" disappearance of the manor and their co-workers drove out any lingering doubts, creating a solid cadre of true believers that formed the seed of a new religion. As worm-touched machines trickled back into base reality, they incorporated them into the growing theology. Today we call them the CotBG.

The main function of the trap itself was to channel the corrupt energy of the worm into the creation of a nearly-alive, self-operating, ever-growing mechanical labyrinth. This "Pipe Nightmare" served as an endless oubliette, a further layer of mechanistic chains on the worm. But the defiling nature of that energy gave the beast ways to reach out from within its prison and twist. It took only a few days to create the infection we call 217 and release it to punish the lesser peons who had a hand in building the trap. It took years of limbo-time before it was able to exert enough influence to convert pieces of the randomly-generating outer prison into a self-sustaining "Factory". With a portion of the constraining energies thus diverted into the creation of reality-defying consumer goods, the worm was able to partially free itself. It was still bound up in the core device, but it at least managed to impinge itself on the prime material plane. Dragging the engine along like steel jaws on the mangled paw of a bear. The violence of that breakout left holes. Holes thru which the Factory could "ship" its "merchandise" and the pipes could blindly grope, probing ever further in search of their lost inmate. Some portions of the prison, more broken than the rest, fell thru those holes. Wherever there is an inexplicable machine, an artillery installation firing infinite mice, or a derelict ship that thinks it is alive, that is a snippet of the prison.

The worm had not neglected vengeance on the man who engineered the snare. For all it strained to subvert the jail, it poured equal measure of hate into grinding his soul between the increasingly corrupted gears of the core. If such a being can be said to regret, it regretted not being able to bring the victim along out of limbo for additional torments. That broken, maddened old man would spread the worm's corruption yet further, reaching out from the industrial limbo-complex to inflict a portion of his own suffering on anyone unfortunate enough to catch his attention. Forever dripping the unclean combination of worm ichor and tainted oil that had soaked his very soul.

item.content:encoded:
The inspiration came to me as I was playing "A Machine for Pigs." I was disappointed with the direction it took. Instead, I started playing out my own plot: "What if they're not on earth anymore?" I thought it would be cool if the big revelation was that they were in some kind of limbo, and the father had teleported the house there so they wouldn't have to live in Victorian London because reasons.

So yes, "A Machine for Pigs" is in there, as well as "The Dark Descent," "Eternal Darkness: Sanity's Requiem," and even some of Stephen King's "The Mist."
